findings.title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns
findings.body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the asynchronous legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is created with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), deriving from the incoming request context. In the Kubernetes API server the request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write completes. The detached goroutine therefore almost always executes with an already-canceled context and the legacy write fails with 'context canceled' — in mode 3 the legacy copy (the stated 'safe measure') is silently skipped, with only a metric recording the failure. The goroutine should first detach values from the request lifecycle, e.g. ctx = context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the 10s timeout.

findings.title: Update passes raw UpdatedObjectInfo to legacy, so UpdatedObject runs twice and the two stores can diverge
findings.body: Update now hands the raw rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update, meaning objInfo.UpdatedObject() is executed independently by each store against its own old object. The previous implementation resolved the object once (Storage.Get + UpdatedObject) and wrapped the result in updateWrapper so both stores persisted the identical object. With the new code, create-on-update paths that generate names/UIDs produce different objects in legacy vs unified storage, and any mutating logic inside UpdatedObject runs twice, so the two stores can silently hold divergent objects — exactly what dual write is meant to prevent. The object should be materialized once and the frozen result passed to the legacy update via updateWrapper, as before.

findings.title: Delete no longer tolerates NotFound from unified storage, so legacy-only objects can never be deleted
findings.body: Delete now returns immediately on any error from unified storage, including NotFound. The previous implementation special-cased apierrors.IsNotFound and still issued the legacy delete. With the new early return, an object that exists only in legacy storage (created before unified storage was enabled, or left behind by a failed dual write) can never be deleted in mode 3: callers receive NotFound and the stale legacy row remains forever.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy API state synchronously, racing the async legacy write
findings.body: The new 'with dual write (file, mode 3)' subtest (line 132) and 'with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)' subtest (line 191) run the full doPlaylistTests suite, which checks legacy API state immediately after k8s writes — e.g. listing /api/playlists right after k8s Create and getFromBothAPIs right after k8s Update. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous (a goroutine with up to a 10s window), so these assertions race it and will flake: the legacy endpoint can still 404 or return the pre-update title. The mode-3 runs need eventually/polling-style assertions for legacy-side reads, or the legacy-side checks should be skipped for mode 3.

findings.title: Delete records storage duration with the object name instead of the kind as metric label
findings.body: On successful Delete, d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name where every other call passes options.Kind as the metric label. Object names (e.g. playlist UIDs) are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus time series — a cardinality explosion — and the metric stops aggregating per kind.

findings.title: Storage create/update failures are recorded in the legacy-duration metric
findings.body: When the unified-storage Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), recording a legacy failure that never happened (legacy is never called on this path) into the legacy duration metric, with the storage start time, and never recording the actual storage failure. The same bug exists in Update at line 129. Both should call d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...). This corrupts the dual-writer metrics that distinguish legacy vs unified errors.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy operation result in the storage-duration metric
findings.body: In DeleteCollection's async goroutine, the outcome of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy), attributing legacy latency and failures to the unified-storage metric. Every other path uses recordLegacyDuration for legacy operations; this should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

findings.title: Delete stores the bare logger (d.Log) in the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: Delete builds a contextual logger with log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then puts the bare logger into the context: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). Downstream log lines emitted from the storage layers lose the name/kind/method identifying fields. It should be klog.NewContext(ctx, log), consistent with the other methods.
